{{Short description|Inverse problem related to neuroscience}}
{{Technical|date=December 2025}}

<!-- Note: The following pages were redirects to [[Inverse recovery in EEG]] before draftification:
*[[Draft:Inverse recovery in EEG]]
-->
The '''inverse recovery in EEG''' is a [[Alberto Calderón|Calderón]]-type [[inverse problem]]<ref>{{cite arXiv | last1=Kian | first1=Yavar | title=Lecture on Calderón problem | date=2019 | class=math.AP | eprint=1909.08939 }}</ref> with the goal of recovering source terms and/or conductivity in layers of the human head from [[Electroencephalography|electroencephalographic]] measurements. Fundamentally, this inverse recovery seeks to solve the [[elliptic partial differential equation]] given by

<math>\nabla \cdot (\sigma \nabla u) = \mathcal{S}</math>     or      <math>\hbox{div }(\sigma \hbox{ grad } u) = \mathcal{S}</math>

where <math>u</math> is the electric potential, <math>\sigma</math> is the (possibly [[Anisotropy|anisotropic]]) conductivity, and <math>\mathcal{S}</math> represents primary current sources in the brain. Depending on the application, the inverse problem consists of either recovering <math>\mathcal{S}</math> from <math>u</math> (the inverse source problem) or recovering <math>\sigma</math> from <math>u</math> (the inverse conductivity problem).

Because the human head is highly inhomogeneous and composed of multiple layers with different conductivities, the inverse EEG problem is severely [[Well-posed problem|ill-posed]] and requires either analytical techniques or numerical approximations to obtain stable solutions (such as the [[finite element method]]).<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Chaddad |first1=Ahmad |last2=Wu |first2=Yihang |last3=Kateb |first3=Reem |last4=Bouridane |first4=Ahmed |date=2023-07-16 |title=Electroencephalography Signal Processing: A Comprehensive Review and Analysis of Methods and Techniques |journal=Sensors |language=en |volume=23 |issue=14 |page=6434 |doi=10.3390/s23146434 |pmid=37514728 |doi-access=free |issn=1424-8220 |pmc=10385593 |bibcode=2023Senso..23.6434C }}</ref>

Due to the form of the governing equation being a sort of "generalization" of the Laplace-Beltrami operator, this problem has deep connections to [[Pseudoanalytic function|generalized analytic function]] theory, [[Thermal conduction|heat conduction]], and broader [[Electromagnetism|electromagnetics]]. In fact, the problem can be seen as solving the [[Poisson's equation|Poisson equation]] for an [[Inhomogeneous electromagnetic wave equation|inhomogeneous]] media, which is indeed how it is derived in the EEG problem.

== Problem derivation ==
An overview on the physical foundations of the problem is given by Darbas and Lohrengel.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Darbas |first1=Marion |last2=Lohrengel |first2=Stephanie |date=2019-03-01 |title=Review on Mathematical Modelling of Electroencephalography (EEG) |journal=Jahresbericht der Deutschen Mathematiker-Vereinigung |language=en |volume=121 |issue=1 |pages=3–39 |doi=10.1365/s13291-018-0183-z |issn=1869-7135}}</ref>

Consider the current density <math>\mathbf{J}(r)</math> produced by neural activity,

<math>\mathbf{J}(r) = \mathbf{J}^p(r)+\sigma(r) \mathbf{E}(r)</math>

where <math>\mathbf{J}^p(r)</math> denotes primary current and <math>\sigma(r)\mathbf{E}(r)</math> the return current (composed of macroscopic conductivity and the brain's electric field). Using the quasi-static approximation of [[Maxwell's equations]],<ref>{{Cite web |last=Haus and Melcher |title=Limits to Statics and Quasistatics |url=https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-007-electromagnetic-energy-from-motors-to-lasers-spring-2011/resources/mit6_007s11_lec17/ |access-date=31 December 2025 |website=MIT OpenCourseWare}}</ref>

<math>\nabla \times \mathbf{E} = 0 \quad \hbox{and} \quad \nabla \cdot \mathbf{J}=0</math>

The first of the above equation implies that the electric field is path-independent and thus we may write <math>\mathbf{E} = -\nabla u</math> with <math>u</math> the electric potential function. Then,

<math>\nabla \cdot (\mathbf{J}^p + \sigma \mathbf{E}) = -\nabla \cdot (\sigma \mathbf{E}) = \nabla \cdot \mathbf{J}^p
</math>

which gives

<math>\nabla \cdot(\sigma \nabla u) = \nabla \cdot \mathbf{J}^p</math>

The primary current is modeled by <math>Q</math> pointwise sources located at some coordinate <math>C_q</math> with dipolar moments <math>p_q</math> (note that <math>p_q</math> is a vector quantity).<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=Grech |first1=Roberta |last2=Cassar |first2=Tracey |last3=Muscat |first3=Joseph |last4=Camilleri |first4=Kenneth P. |last5=Fabri |first5=Simon G. |last6=Zervakis |first6=Michalis |last7=Xanthopoulos |first7=Petros |last8=Sakkalis |first8=Vangelis |last9=Vanrumste |first9=Bart |date=2008-11-07 |title=Review on solving the inverse problem in EEG source analysis |journal=Journal of Neuroengineering and Rehabilitation |volume=5 |article-number=25 |doi=10.1186/1743-0003-5-25 |doi-access=free |issn=1743-0003 |pmc=2605581 |pmid=18990257}}</ref> Using the [[Dirac delta function|Dirac delta]] distribution,

<math>\mathbf{J}^p = \sum_{q=1}^Q p_q \delta_{C_q}</math>

Thus, the source term is

<math>\mathcal{S} := \nabla \mathbf{J}^p = \sum_{q=1}^Q p_q \cdot \nabla \delta_{C_q}</math>.

== Exact solutions ==

=== Constant conductivity ===
Many analytical studies assume that conductivity is piecewise constant in layers representing the brain, skull, and scalp.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2" /><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Paraskevopoulou |first1=Georgina |last2=Fokas |first2=Athanassios S. |last3=Charalambopoulos |first3=Antonios |last4=Perantonis |first4=Stavros |date=2023 |editor-last=Bountis |editor-first=Tassos |chapter=Correction to: Inverse EEG Problem, Minimization and Numerical Solutions |series=Springer Proceedings in Complexity |editor2-last=Vallianatos |editor2-first=Filippos |editor3-last=Provata |editor3-first=Astero |editor4-last=Kugiumtzis |editor4-first=Dimitris |editor5-last=Kominis |editor5-first=Yannis |title=Chaos, Fractals and Complexity |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-37404-3_26 |language=en |location=Cham |publisher=Springer International Publishing |pages=C1 |doi=10.1007/978-3-031-37404-3_26 |isbn=978-3-031-37404-3}}</ref> Let <math>\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^3</math> denote the head domain decomposed into three concentric spherical domains <math>\Omega_i,\,i=0,1,2</math>, where <math>\Omega_0</math> is a ball and <math>\Omega_1,\Omega_2</math> are spherical shells. When <math>\sigma</math> is assumed piecewise constant, the governing equation reduces to a set of Laplace and Poisson equations:<ref name=":2" />

<math>\begin{cases}
\Delta u = 0 & \text{on} \quad \Omega_1,\Omega_2\\
\Delta u = \displaystyle \frac{1}{\sigma_0}\sum_{q=1}^{Q}p_q\cdot \nabla \delta_{C_q} & \text{on} \quad \Omega_0\\
u = g & \text{on} \quad \partial\Omega
\end{cases}</math>

Solutions can be obtained using [[Green's function]]s, spherical harmonics, and separation of variables.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Green |first1=George |last2=Wheelhouse |first2=T. |last3=Lindsay |first3=R. Bruce |date=1959-10-01 |title=An Essay on the Application of Mathematical Analysis to the Theories of Electricity and Magnetism |journal=Physics Today |volume=12 |issue=10 |page=48 |doi=10.1063/1.3060521 |bibcode=1959PhT....12j..48G |issn=0031-9228}}</ref>

A benchmark tool in the problem of piecewise constant conductivity is FindSource3D,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Clerc |first1=M |last2=Leblond |first2=J |last3=Marmorat |first3=J-P |last4=Papadopoulo |first4=T |date=2012-04-23 |title=Source localization using rational approximation on plane sections |journal=Inverse Problems |volume=28 |issue=5 |article-number=055018 |doi=10.1088/0266-5611/28/5/055018 |bibcode=2012InvPr..28e5018C |issn=0266-5611}}</ref> a source localization tool which has shown perfect reconstruction when negligible error is assumed in source location. Such a tool has also been used for conductivity reconstruction, again with perfect accuracy under suitable error assumptions.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last1=Clerc |first1=Maureen |last2=Leblond |first2=Juliette |last3=Marmorat |first3=Jean-Paul |last4=Papageorgakis |first4=Christos |date=2016 |title=Uniqueness result for an inverse conductivity recovery problem with application to EEG. |url=https://hal.science/hal-01303640v2 |journal=Rendiconti dell'Istituto di Matematica dell'Universita di Trieste|volume=48}}</ref>

=== Non-constant conductivity ===
For non-constant or anisotropic conductivity, the inverse problem becomes substantially more difficult.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Marin |first1=Gildas |last2=Guerin |first2=Christophe |last3=Baillet |first3=Sylvain |last4=Garnero |first4=Line |last5=Meunier |first5=Gérard |date=1998 |title=Influence of skull anisotropy for the forward and inverse problem in EEG: Simulation studies using FEM on realistic head models |journal=Human Brain Mapping |language=en |volume=6 |issue=4 |pages=250–269 |doi=10.1002/(SICI)1097-0193(1998)6:4<250::AID-HBM5>3.0.CO;2-2 |pmid=9704264 |pmc=6873358 }}</ref> Classical uniqueness and stability results for Calderón-type inverse problems apply under varying regularity assumptions on the boundary of <math>\Omega</math>; for example, Alessandrini established uniqueness with [[Lipschitz domain|Lipschitz boundaries]], while Kohn and Vogelius proved stability under smooth boundary conditions.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Alessandrini |first=Giovanni |date=April 1990 |title=Singular solutions of elliptic equations and the determination of conductivity by boundary measurements |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/0022039690900784 |journal=Journal of Differential Equations |language=en |volume=84 |issue=2 |pages=252–272 |doi=10.1016/0022-0396(90)90078-4 |bibcode=1990JDE....84..252A |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Alessandrini |first=Giovanni |date=1988-01-01 |title=Stable determination of conductivity by boundary measurements |journal=Applicable Analysis |volume=27 |issue=1–3 |pages=153–172 |doi=10.1080/00036818808839730 |issn=0003-6811}}</ref>

Exact solutions for spatially varying <math>\sigma</math> are generally unavailable. Modern work therefore typically focuses on [[Perturbation theory|perturbative]] methods, [[integral equation]] formulations, or regularization techniques for ensuring stable recovery.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last1=Elvetun |first1=Ole Løseth |last2=Sudheer |first2=Niranjana |date=2025-09-01 |title=Weighted sparsity regularization for solving the inverse EEG problem: A case study |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1746809425001843 |journal=Biomedical Signal Processing and Control |volume=107 |article-number=107673 |doi=10.1016/j.bspc.2025.107673 |issn=1746-8094|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Johnson |first=S.G. |date=2010 |title=Notes on Green's functions in inhomogeneous media |url=https://math.mit.edu/~stevenj/18.303/inhomog-notes.pdf |access-date=31 December 2025 |website=MIT OpenCourseWare}}</ref>

== Numerical solutions ==
Because analytical solutions are available only in highly idealized geometries, numerical methods play a central role in practical EEG inverse recovery. Common approaches include typical Finite Element or [[Boundary element method|Boundary Element Methods]].<ref name=":3" />

Numerical inverse recovery typically requires regularization methods such as Tikhonov regularization, sparsity constraints, or Bayesian inverse modeling to counteract ill-posedness.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Tikhonov |first=Andrey |date=1943 |title=Об устойчивости обратных задач |journal=Doklady Akademii Nauk SSSR |volume=39 |pages=195–198}}</ref> Practical EEG systems also incorporate noise modeling and electrode placement uncertainty.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Nüßing |first=Andreas |date=2018 |title=Fitted and Unitted Finite Element Methods for Solving the EEG Forward Problem |url=https://nbn-resolving.de/urn:nbn:de:hbz:6-67139436770 |journal=Doctoral Dissertation |via=Publication server of the University of Münster}}</ref>
